doc.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: How music training helps in a band
summary: Her choral training lets her match a horn player's vibrato, breathing and phrasing and feel as one unit.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Having — being educated in music, does it help you in a band situation because you know — I’m trying to figure out how to say this correctly. You know chords and you know forms, perhaps more than some singers who are sort of just singing innately. Is it helpful to you that you have that music education background?

Oh yes, yes, yes. Very much so. Because there are just little things that I learned in the training that I use. For instance if I’m doing harmony with the horn player and he’s using a vibrato, okay, then I think that I should match his vibrato to make it even closer. You know? And I’ll listen to his breathing, where he’s phrasing, so that we can phrase alike. So much of this stuff happens, you know, it’s impromptu, you know, it’s improvisational. So to make it sound more like a unit and all of this, those are the little things that I listen for. Had I not had the training in choral singing and breathing and phrasing and listening — because I used to play bass you know — and listening to the bands and all of this and what the people were doing, I don’t think I would be as aware, you know, of those little secrets. Sometimes if we’re doing a tune and maybe we’re not doing it exactly as it’s supposed to be rhythmically, but I’ll listen to what the horn guy is doing and if he’s going to do a little syncopated thing instead of right on, I’m going to match that, I’m going to work with that. Because it’s all about making the music. It’s all about making the music and making that sound you know. And it’s all about — how shall I say — experiencing a oneness.
